prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayers at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, founding moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a case where a minimal continuum model (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) predicted a specific, quantitative mechanism, namely interlayer tunnelling flattening the bands at a small twist angle, and where the 2018 experiments by Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at exactly that angle. It is a rare instance of a simple mechanism that is understood and not only observed, and it has spawned moire physics in many other materials (transition-metal dichalcogenides, fractional Chern insulators, twistronics). The theory-plus-experiment structure maps onto the three credited names without strain.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the many-body physics: the origin of the superconductivity and the nature of the correlated phases are still debated, sample-to-sample variation is large, and so the prize would honour the single-particle flat-band mechanism plus an experimental discovery whose interpretation is open. Attribution is also imperfect: Yuan Cao, the first author of the 2018 papers, and independent groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others) are outside a three-name limit, and Bistritzer's share relative to others who contributed to the flat-band theory is a judgement call. The optical lattice clock (B015) has far cleaner attribution and stronger agreement among colleagues.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first for a clean idea, robust and reproduced result and two-name attribution, and regards magic-angle graphene as somewhat early because the many-body physics and the origin of superconductivity are unsettled.
responses.response: I accept that the clock has the cleaner attribution and the more settled interpretation, which is why I keep B015 as an alternative and rank it above everything outside the condensed-matter group. But I distinguish what is being honoured. The prize would go to the flat-band mechanism and the discovery of the correlated phases, both secure, not to a theory of the superconductivity. A discovery whose application and interpretation keep evolving can still be mature, as was the case for earlier discoveries in the field. I also note that you rank Kane-Mele-Molenkamp above moire graphene, and I agree it is a strong, mature candidate.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as the clearest recent theory-followed-by-experiment case with quantitative links to transport and spectroscopy, while conceding timing may be early and that the first author of the experiment and other groups complicate fairness.
responses.response: I share your view of the physics and I think your point about quantitative modelling is the strongest argument. I would add that the credit problem is not only about Cao: it also concerns whether the prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald, rather than the broader theory community, is the right anchor. Where we may differ is that I would not regard the open pairing mechanism as a reason to wait, because delay does not make the attribution problem easier, and I am wary of leaving the three-name restriction as the only guide to who gets credited.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a genuine clue from nature that opened neutrino astronomy and is strongly confirmed, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene third, noting the junior experimentalists left off the list.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube opened a real new window and that the diffuse flux is solid. My reservation is attribution rather than merit: the discovery rests on a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage, and the decisive roles of Halzen, Karle and Spiering are hard to separate on the evidence in front of us (Olsson would credit only two of them). For graphene the same junior-author problem you raise exists, but the discovery paper has a clearer small set of originators, one theoretical and one experimental, so I find the allocation easier to defend.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a genuine invention that changed an entire instrument class and is overdue, while flagging her own possible subject bias.
responses.response: I respect the invention and the maturity, and I appreciate the candour about bias. My concern is that the prize would honour an enabling technology whose scientific consequences are spread over many fields, with a real credit issue involving the STEM corrector line of Krivanek and Dellby. I weigh a discovery that generated a new field of physics, with a mechanism that is simple and general, more heavily than an instrument, though I accept that the instrument case is not weak and deserves a hearing, so I would not oppose it as part of a split.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unsettled superconducting pairing mechanism as a reason for delay, or the single-particle flat-band prediction plus the experimental discovery as sufficient.
Whether Bistritzer should be credited alongside MacDonald, and how to handle the first author Yuan Cao and independent groups within a three-person limit.
Whether the 2016 topological-phase prize reduces the appetite for B055, and whether the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize makes B024 unattractive.
My memory of the early history (priority among theory contributions and parallel experiments) is not verified against sources here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate, and I note only that I am a theorist in the same broad community as MacDonald's flat-band work without direct ties, and I share a Gothenburg environment with colleagues Johansson and Olsson, which is not relevant to these candidates beyond B024 and B013.
